learn: Every player has a role: melody, harmony, bass line or rhythm.
Section leaders guide their sections; the conductor unifies the whole.
Knowing your role helps balance.
lessons.try: Mark your part's role in each section of a piece.

learn: Arrive early, prepared, with pencil and music.
Mark the score with reminders.
Practise your part between rehearsals.
lessons.try: Create a personal practice schedule for your part.

learn: Listen across the group, not just to yourself.
Match style, dynamics and articulation with others.
Blend means no single voice sticks out unless it should.
lessons.try: Play a passage while focusing on a different section each time.

learn: Good posture opens the airway and supports breathing.
Diaphragmatic breathing gives steady air.
Breath support controls tone and phrasing.
lessons.try: Practise breathing exercises for five minutes daily.

learn: Every instrument and voice has a characteristic tone.
Long tones build control and consistency.
Listen to professional recordings as models.
lessons.try: Record long tones and compare them to a professional model.

learn: Keep tone full at soft dynamics and controlled at loud dynamics.
Avoid forcing at fortissimo.
Crescendo and diminuendo shape phrases.
lessons.try: Practise a scale from pianissimo to fortissimo and back.

learn: Intonation is playing or singing in tune.
Bands tune to concert B-flat; orchestras to A (usually 440 Hz).
Temperature and fatigue affect pitch.
lessons.try: Tune with a tuner, then by ear.

learn: Beats (wavering) mean pitches are slightly apart.
Adjust until the beats disappear.
Unisons and octaves are easiest to hear.
check: The easiest intervals to tune are...
lessons.try: Tune a unison with a partner by listening for beats.

learn: In just tuning, major thirds are slightly lowered and fifths slightly raised compared to equal temperament.
Tune from the bass up.
Locked-in chords "ring".
check: In just tuning, major thirds are slightly...
lessons.try: Tune a sustained chord as an ensemble.

learn: A steady internal pulse keeps the ensemble together.
Subdivide beats to place notes precisely.
Practise with a metronome.
lessons.try: Play a passage with a metronome on beats 2 and 4.

learn: Mixed meters (5/8, 7/8) group beats unevenly: 2+3 or 3+2+2.
Leonard Bernstein's "America" alternates 6/8 and 3/4.
Count groupings aloud.
lessons.try: Clap a 7/8 pattern grouped 2+2+3.

learn: Swing, straight, laid-back and driving feels.
Rhythmic feel varies by genre.
Lock in with the rhythm section.
lessons.try: Play a melody straight, then swung.

learn: Check key, time signature, tempo, repeats and tricky passages.
Scan for accidentals and dynamics.
Silently finger or hum through the music.
lessons.try: Use a 30-second scan routine before sight-reading.

learn: Keep going; don't stop for mistakes.
Read ahead of where you're playing.
Prioritise rhythm over notes.
lessons.try: Sight-read a new piece daily for two weeks.

learn: Sight-reading improves with daily practice.
Start with easy music and increase difficulty.
Recognise common patterns: scales, arpeggios, rhythms.
lessons.try: Track sight-reading progress for a month.

learn: Identify intervals by sound.
Recognise major, minor, diminished and augmented triads.
Use reference songs to remember intervals.
lessons.try: Take a daily interval quiz for two weeks.

learn: Dictation means writing down music you hear.
Start by finding the tonic, then contour, then rhythm.
Practise with short phrases.
lessons.try: Notate four-bar melodies by ear.

learn: Hear bass lines and chord changes.
Identify cadences by ear.
Sing chord roots while listening.
lessons.try: Identify I, IV and V chords in a song by ear.

learn: Patterns: two (down-up), three (down-right-up), four (down-left-right-up).
The right hand keeps time; the left hand shows expression.
The preparatory beat sets tempo and breath.
lessons.try: Conduct a recording in 3/4 and 4/4.

learn: Scores list instruments in families: woodwinds, brass, percussion, strings.
Transposing instruments are written at different pitches.
Follow multiple lines at once.
lessons.try: Follow a full score while listening to a recording.

learn: Plan rehearsal goals and timing.
Give clear, specific feedback.
Model what you want.
lessons.try: Lead a five-minute sectional rehearsal.

learn: Baroque: light articulation, terraced dynamics, ornaments.
Classical: clarity and balance. Romantic: expressive rubato and rich tone.
Research performance practice.
lessons.try: Play a passage in Baroque and Romantic style.

learn: Interpretation is making musical choices within the composer's markings.
Shape phrases with dynamics, timing and tone.
Compare recordings by different performers.
lessons.try: Compare three recordings of the same piece.

learn: Jazz, gospel, Latin, folk and world music each have stylistic conventions.
Learn styles from listening and from tradition bearers.
Respect cultural origins.
lessons.try: Learn a piece in an unfamiliar style.

learn: Chamber music has one player per part: duos, trios, quartets, quintets.
Players lead each other without a conductor.
Cueing with breath and eye contact keeps the group together.
check: Chamber music has ___ player per part.
lessons.try: Rehearse a short chamber piece in a small group.

learn: Warm up, target problem spots, then play through.
Slow practice fixes difficult passages.
End positively.
lessons.try: Plan and run a 20-minute sectional.

learn: Leaders listen, encourage and set an example.
Resolve disagreements respectfully.
Shared goals unite the ensemble.
lessons.try: Reflect on a time you led or followed well.

learn: Plan practice backward from the concert date.
Mock performances build confidence.
Manage nerves with breathing and routine.
lessons.try: Give a mock performance for friends.

learn: Choose repertoire that shows your growth.
Write programme notes about each piece.
Stage presence: walk on confidently, bow, acknowledge accompanists.
lessons.try: Perform your capstone concert.

learn: Paths: music degrees, community ensembles, teaching, recording, music therapy.
Lifelong music-making enriches life.
Keep playing, singing and listening.
lessons.try: Research ensembles you could join after graduation.
